name: Nanofat / fat grafting tear trough

card.summary: The patient's own fat, moved into under-eye hollows; longer-lasting in theory, with sparse tear-trough-specific trial data.
card.aka: Autologous fat transfer, lipofilling, periorbital fat grafting
card.note: Fat necrosis, reabsorption and contour irregularities are documented; embolic complications are described with autologous fat.

quick.overview:
Fat grafting takes fat from elsewhere on the body, usually by liposuction, processes it and injects it into areas that have lost volume. In the under-eye region it is used to soften hollows where the lower eyelid meets the cheek. Nanofat refers to fat that has been broken down into a finer emulsion, which proponents describe as useful for thin skin.

It is a surgical procedure rather than a product, and it is discussed in appearance communities as an alternative to hyaluronic acid filler because the material is the patient's own tissue. Published tear-trough-specific trials are scarce.
quick.mechanism: Fat is harvested, handled to preserve cell survival, and re-injected into the target area to add volume. Some of it is reabsorbed, and reports describe stem-cell-related regenerative effects as a rationale for finer preparations such as nanofat.
quick.risks: Reported risks include swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain, infection, lumps or contour irregularity, fat necrosis and variable reabsorption. Embolic complications, including rare vision loss, are described with injectable materials and have been linked more often to autologous fat than to hyaluronic acid.

lead: Fat grafting, also called autologous fat transfer or lipofilling, is a procedure in which fat taken from one part of the body is processed and injected into another to restore volume or improve contour.[1] In the face it is used in several regions, including the lower eyelid and cheek junction (the tear trough), where hollowing is a common concern.[1]

The term nanofat describes fat that has been mechanically emulsified into a fine preparation, which proponents describe as useful for superficial or thin skin because of its stem-cell content.[1] Wikipedia notes that the regenerative potential of fat has been a research subject since studies of adipose-derived stem cells in the early 2000s.[1]
The wiki's source base for this entry is thin. One registered trial examined activated platelet-rich plasma added to fat transfer, but no trial specific to nanofat in the tear trough was found.[2]

paras: The procedure has three stages: harvesting fat, often by liposuction, processing it, and injecting it into the target area.[1] Sources describe minimizing handling and re-injecting promptly to preserve graft survival.[1]

Besides breast and buttock work, fat grafting is used for facial volume restoration, including periorbital contour and volume loss.[1] A 2021 paper by Marten and Elyassnia on periorbital fat grafting is among the sources cited by Wikipedia.[1]

Listed complications include swelling, bruising, hematoma, paresthesia or donor-site pain, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities and injury from cannulas.[1] Fat necrosis and reabsorption are recognized concerns; Wikipedia cites reabsorption of up to about 50 percent in breast augmentation.[1]

Separately, an overview of injectable fillers states that rare blindness and delayed skin necrosis can follow embolization of injected material, and that necrosis is more often linked to autologous fat than to hyaluronic acid.[3]

No studies found on nanofat or fat grafting specifically for the tear trough among the sources reviewed. A completed phase 2/3 registration (NCT01461785, n=25, started 2012) evaluated activated platelet-rich plasma in human autologous fat transfer, a related but different question.[2]

refs.title: The Use of Activated Platelet Rich Plasma (PRP) in Human Autologous Fat Transfer
